Amillennialists (Augustine, Hoekema, Riddlebarger, Storms, Beale) see 20:1-6 as a recapitulation that returns to Christ's first coming: Satan was bound at the cross so that he cannot deceive the nations or stop the gospel; the first resurrection is the believer's new life or entry into heaven at death; the thousand years symbolise the whole church age; and Satan's release, Gog and Magog, the Second Coming, a single general resurrection and the final judgment come together at the end. Critics argue the binding language is too strong for the present age; proponents respond that it is restricted to deceiving the nations.

Historic premillennialists (Justin, Irenaeus, Ladd, Blomberg) read 19-20 sequentially: Christ returns, Satan is bound, the righteous are bodily raised and reign with Christ on earth for an extended (perhaps symbolic) period, after which Satan's final revolt is crushed, the rest of the dead are raised, and the final judgment and new creation follow. The church passes through the tribulation; there is no separate Israel programme. Critics point to New Testament texts that link one resurrection and judgment to one return; proponents point to the two uses of 'came to life' in 20:4-5.

Dispensational premillennialists (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie, Ice) see a literal 1,000-year earthly kingdom following the Second Coming, in which Christ reigns from Jerusalem, Israel enjoys the fulfilment of its national covenants, glorified saints rule with him, and people born in natural bodies populate the earth; Satan is totally confined, released at the end for a last rebellion, and then the great white throne judges the unbelieving dead. Critics charge that this is the only explicit mention of a millennium; proponents answer that it is the climax of many Old Testament kingdom prophecies.

Partial preterists hold that most of Revelation (through the fall of Jerusalem) was fulfilled in the first century but that chapter 20 reaches beyond it. Most are postmillennial (Chilton, Gentry, DeMar) — the millennium is the present age of Christ's reign since his ascension and the judgment of AD 70, ending in the future Second Coming and final judgment — while some are amillennial. They emphatically affirm a future bodily resurrection and final judgment (20:11-15).

Full preterists (Russell, Max King, Don Preston) usually place the millennium between Christ's ministry or cross and AD 70, identifying Satan's release and Gog-Magog with the Jewish War and the great white throne with the judgment of AD 70; the resurrection is corporate and covenantal. Because this denies a future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment, it is outside the historic creeds (as critics including partial preterists like Gentry stress); proponents respond that the creeds must yield to Scripture's time statements.

Historicists varied: many older ones followed Augustine's reading, dating the binding to Constantine's victory over paganism and the release to the rise of Islam or the papacy; nineteenth-century historicists (Elliott, many Adventist and premillennial writers) expected a future millennium after the fall of papal Rome, while others (Barnes) expected a future postmillennial era of gospel triumph.

Futurists, usually premillennial, read the chapter as following the Second Coming chronologically: future binding, resurrection of the righteous, earthly reign, final revolt and final judgment. The phrase 'Then I saw' and the reference back to the beast and false prophet already in the lake (20:10) are taken as markers of sequence.

Idealists (Hendriksen, Milligan) read chapter 20 as the seventh and final cycle of the book, starting again from Christ's first coming: the binding is Satan's defeat at the cross, the reign is the church's victorious life with Christ, the release is the final apostasy, and the white throne is the last judgment — a timeless assurance that martyrdom ends in enthronement.

Eclectic commentators divide: Osborne and Mounce lean premillennial, reading the binding and first resurrection as future, while recognising symbolic numbers and first-century background; Keener and others weigh amillennial arguments more sympathetically while finding the premillennial reading of 20:4-5 strongest.
Does 20:1-3 describe a binding that has already happened, or one still future? Compare Matthew 12:29, Luke 10:18 and 1 Peter 5:8.
Can 'came to life' mean different things in 20:4 and 20:5? How do John 5:25-29 and 1 Corinthians 15:23-24 affect your answer?
Why might the thousand years be symbolic in a book full of symbolic numbers — or why might it be literal?
Compare 19:17-21 with 20:7-10 and Ezekiel 38-39. One battle or two?
How does the great white throne combine judgment by deeds with the Book of Life?
A New Heaven and a New Earth: The Bride, the Holy City
The new creation and the New Jerusalem (21:1-22:5)

John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with the sea no more, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God as a bride adorned for her husband. A voice from the throne announces that God's dwelling is now with humanity, that he will wipe away every tear and end death and mourning, and the One on the throne declares 'I make all things new', offering the water of life freely to the thirsty while warning that the unfaithful have their part in the second death. One of the bowl angels then carries John to a great, high mountain to see the bride: a radiant city with a high wall, twelve gates named for Israel's tribes, twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles, perfectly cubic in shape (12,000 stadia each way), built of gold clear as glass, its foundations adorned with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl. There is no temple in it, because God and the Lamb are its temple, and no need of sun or moon; the nations walk by its light and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, but nothing unclean enters.
New heaven, new earth, no sea; the new Jerusalem descends as a bride
God's dwelling with humanity; tears, death and pain ended
'I make all things new': the water of life for the thirsty, the second death for the unfaithful
The bride-city seen from a high mountain: wall, twelve gates, twelve foundations
The city measured: a cube of 12,000 stadia, a wall of 144 cubits
Materials of glory: jasper wall, gold city, twelve jewelled foundations, pearl gates
No temple, no sun, no night; the glory of the nations brought in

The vision fuses the great hopes of the prophets. Isaiah promised new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem created for joy (Isaiah 65:17-25; 66:22) and pictured Zion rebuilt with jewelled foundations, gates and walls (Isaiah 54:11-12), radiant with God's glory so that sun and moon are unnecessary, its gates always open to receive the wealth of the nations (Isaiah 60). Ezekiel 40-48 gave the blueprint of a restored temple-city whose gates carry the names of the twelve tribes and whose name is 'The LORD is there' (Ezekiel 48:30-35). Second Temple Judaism multiplied these hopes: Tobit 13:16-18 describes a Jerusalem built of sapphire and emerald with walls of precious stone and towers of gold; 4 Ezra 9-10 has a mourning woman transformed before the seer's eyes into a city with great foundations; 2 Baruch 4:2-6 speaks of a heavenly city prepared beforehand and shown to Adam, Abraham and Moses; and the Aramaic 'New Jerusalem' texts from Qumran (4Q554-555, 5Q15, 11Q18) record an angel measuring a huge city with twelve gates named after the tribes. 1 Enoch 90:28-29 imagines God replacing the old 'house' with a new and greater one. Paul and Hebrews speak of the Jerusalem above (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 11:10, 16; 12:22).

John's first audience lived in proud Hellenistic cities — Ephesus with its temple of Artemis, Pergamum with its acropolis of temples, Laodicea with its wealth — and in an empire whose capital called itself eternal. Ancient writers described great cities by their walls, gates and dimensions; Herodotus famously described Babylon as a square city (1.178-181). Precious stones, gold and pearls were the costliest luxury goods of the Roman world (Pliny, Natural History 9 and 37), precisely the cargo of fallen Babylon (18:12-16). The bride-city answers the prostitute-city point by point: both are shown by one of the bowl angels (17:1; 21:9), both are adorned with gold, jewels and pearls, but one is drunk on the blood of the saints and the other is the holy dwelling of God. Interpreters disagree on whether the city is a literal future metropolis, a symbolic portrait of the glorified people of God (Gundry's 'people as place'), the consummated new creation, or — in some preterist and postmillennial readings — the new covenant church already descending since the fall of earthly Jerusalem.
A new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away

Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth; 1 Enoch 45:4-5 and 91:16 foresee a transformed heaven and earth; Jubilees 1:29 looks to the day of the new creation; 2 Baruch 32:6 and 4 Ezra 7:75 speak of creation renewed. Psalm 102:25-27 contrasts the perishing creation with the unchanging God.

Stoic philosophy taught a cyclic conflagration (ekpyrōsis) and rebirth of the cosmos; Roman propaganda celebrated a renewed age under the emperors. John's new creation is a once-for-all act of God, not a cycle.

The Greek kainos suggests newness of quality rather than an entirely different thing, and most current interpreters see renewal and transformation of the cosmos (Romans 8:19-23) rather than annihilation and replacement, though both views have defenders (2 Peter 3:10-13 is read both ways). The 'first' heaven and earth is the old order marked by sin and death.
Futurists place this after the millennium and the great white throne as the eternal state; dispensationalists (Walvoord) often see a literal renovation by fire (2 Peter 3:10).
Amillennialists (Hoekema, Beale) see the renewed cosmos that immediately follows the single Second Coming and general judgment, the final goal of redemption.

Some partial preterists (Chilton, and in part Gentry) note that the new creation has begun in the new covenant (2 Corinthians 5:17; Isaiah 65 includes death and childbearing), so that 21-22 portrays the church's present glory flowing into its final consummation.

Full preterists identify the new heavens and earth with the new covenant order fully established when the old covenant 'world' (temple and Jerusalem) passed away in AD 70; critics respond that Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3 promise a renewal of the physical creation still awaited, while proponents reply that 'heaven and earth' in prophetic usage can denote a covenant order (Isaiah 51:15-16; 65:17-18).
Historicists (Barnes, Elliott) generally place the new creation after the millennium and final judgment, as the eternal state that ends the prophetic history of the church.
And the sea was no more

In the Old Testament the sea symbolises chaos and hostile powers: the deep of Genesis 1:2, the sea-monsters Rahab and Leviathan crushed by God (Psalm 74:13-14; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9-10), and the restless wicked (Isaiah 57:20). Daniel's beasts rise from the sea (Daniel 7:2-3). Testament of Moses 10:6 says at the end the sea will retreat into the abyss; Sibylline Oracles 5.447 speaks of the sea drying up.
For John on Patmos the sea separated him from the churches; it was also the highway of Rome's commerce (18:17-19) and the direction from which Roman governors arrived in Asia.

Not a statement about geography but about the end of everything the sea stood for: chaos, the source of the beast (13:1), death (20:13), separation and the trade of Babylon. It is the first of a series of 'no mores' (21:4; 22:3, 5).
Some literal futurists take it as a physical change in the new earth (no oceans); many futurists also accept its symbolic force.
Idealists and most commentators read it symbolically as the abolition of chaos, evil and separation.
The holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God

Isaiah 52:1 and 60-62 promise a glorified Zion; Ezekiel 40-48 describes a restored temple-city. Tobit 13:16-18; 4 Ezra 7:26 and 10:25-59 (the woman who becomes a city 'not built by human hands'); 2 Baruch 4:2-6 (a pre-existent city shown to Adam, Abraham and Moses); and the Qumran 'New Jerusalem' texts all anticipate a city from God. Galatians 4:26 and Hebrews 12:22 speak of the heavenly Jerusalem.
Hellenistic and Roman civic pride centred on city foundations, walls and gates; many cities in Asia Minor claimed divine founders. Rome called itself the eternal city.

The city comes 'down', from God: it is gift, not human achievement — the opposite of Babel/Babylon. It is simultaneously a city, a bride (21:2, 9) and a temple (21:22). Many recent commentators follow Gundry in seeing the city primarily as the glorified people of God themselves, while others insist on a real place for real resurrected people (or both).

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) understand a literal city, the eternal home of the redeemed; Pentecost argued that it exists above the earth during the millennium as the dwelling of resurrected saints and then descends to the new earth.
Amillennialists (Beale, Hoekema) see the consummated people of God and new creation pictured as the Edenic temple-city filling the whole earth.

Chilton reads the new Jerusalem as the church, already come down from heaven in the new covenant and replacing apostate earthly Jerusalem after AD 70 (compare Hebrews 12:22), with its fullness yet to come; Gentry likewise stresses its 'already' dimension while affirming future consummation.
Idealists portray the ideal church — God's people as his dwelling — glimpsed now and perfected at the end.
Full preterists view the city as the new covenant community fully established at AD 70, now present as God's dwelling with his people.
Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband

Isaiah 61:10 (a bride adorned with jewels); Isaiah 62:5 (as a bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so God over Zion); Isaiah 49:18 (Zion wearing her children as bridal ornaments). 4 Ezra 10 merges woman and city. Joseph and Aseneth 15 depicts Aseneth's bridal adornment as a City of Refuge.
The adornment (kosmeō, the root of 'cosmetic') of a Greco-Roman bride was a public display of honour; the harlot is also adorned (17:4), but with stolen luxury.

Completes the marriage announced in 19:7-9. The bride-city is the faithful people of God in covenant intimacy with the Lamb, the antithesis of the harlot-city. The same angel type who showed John the harlot (17:1) now shows the bride (21:9).
Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man… They will be His people

The Greek skēnē ('tent, tabernacle') and verb skēnoō echo the Hebrew mishkan and the later rabbinic term Shekinah for God's dwelling presence. The covenant formula 'I will put my dwelling among you… and you shall be my people' (Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; Jeremiah 31:33; Zechariah 2:10-11; 8:8) is fulfilled. Exodus 25:8 grounds the tabernacle in God's desire to dwell among Israel.

The goal of the whole biblical story: God dwelling with his people as in Eden, the tabernacle and the incarnation (John 1:14). Significant manuscripts read 'peoples' (laoi), which would extend Israel's covenant identity to the redeemed of all nations — a textual variant many commentators (Bauckham, Beale) consider original.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes… no more death or mourning or crying or pain

Isaiah 25:8 (God swallows up death and wipes tears from all faces); Isaiah 35:10 and 65:19 (no more sound of weeping in Jerusalem). 2 Baruch 73:2-3 and 1 Enoch 25:6 envisage a world without pain or sorrow.
Funeral lament and professional mourners were constant features of ancient city life; inscriptions on tombs often expressed hopelessness about death.
The tender gesture of God himself, repeating the promise of 7:17. 'The former things have passed away' echoes Isaiah 65:16-17. Death, the last enemy, is gone (20:14).
Behold, I make all things new
Isaiah 43:18-19 ('Behold, I am doing a new thing') in the context of a new exodus; Isaiah 65:17. 1 Enoch 45:4-5 has God transforming heaven and earth.

The first direct speech of God from the throne since 1:8. The present tense ('I am making') has led some to see the renewal as already underway in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), consummated at the end. Not 'all new things' but 'all things new' — renewal of the existing creation.
It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End

Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12: the LORD is the first and the last. A later rabbinic saying (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a) calls truth (emet: aleph, mem, tav — first, middle and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet) the seal of God; this is late but shows similar alphabet symbolism.
Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet; letters were also used in Greek magic and numerology. The phrase claims the whole of reality from beginning to end.

'It is done' (gegonan, plural 'they are done') echoes the seventh bowl (16:17) and recalls Jesus' 'It is finished' (John 19:30). God, who began history, now completes it. The same title is used of Jesus in 22:13, a strong statement of his deity.
To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life

Isaiah 55:1 ('come to the waters… without money'); Isaiah 12:3 (wells of salvation); Jeremiah 2:13 (God the fountain of living waters); Psalm 36:9; Zechariah 14:8. 1 Enoch 48:1 describes a fountain of righteousness from which the thirsty drink.

Water supply was a constant urban concern in Asia Minor; Laodicea depended on piped water that arrived tepid (3:16), and civic fountains (nymphaea) were monuments of imperial benefaction. Here water is given 'freely' (dōrean), not as patronage.
Eternal life is a free gift to all who long for it, anticipating the river of 22:1 and the invitation of 22:17; it also echoes Jesus' offer of living water (John 4:10-14; 7:37-39).
The one who overcomes will inherit all things… he will be My son

The Davidic covenant promise, 'I will be his father and he shall be my son' (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7; 89:26-27), is here extended to every faithful believer. Inheritance of the land (Psalm 37:11; Isaiah 60:21) becomes inheritance of the whole new creation. Jubilees 1:24-25 promises that Israel will be called children of the living God.
In Roman law an adopted son received full rights of inheritance — imagery used by Paul (Romans 8:15-17; Galatians 4:5-7).
The only place in Revelation where God calls a believer 'my son'. It gathers up all the promises to the overcomers in the seven letters (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21).
The cowardly and unbelieving and abominable… their place will be in the lake that burns
Vice lists were common in Jewish ethical teaching (Wisdom of Solomon 14:22-27 links idolatry with murder, adultery and deceit). Deuteronomy 20:8 sends the fainthearted home from holy war.

Pliny's letter to Trajan (Letters 10.96) describes some who had once confessed Christ but under examination cursed Christ and offered to the emperor's image — the kind of 'cowardice' Revelation warns against.

The list heads with 'cowardly' and 'unbelieving' (or 'unfaithful'), aimed at professing believers tempted to compromise under pressure, not only pagan outsiders. The promise and warning together function as an appeal to the churches.
He carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high

Ezekiel was brought in visions to a very high mountain to see the city-temple (Ezekiel 40:2). Zion is raised above all mountains (Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4:1). Eden was on the mountain of God (Ezekiel 28:13-16). 1 Enoch 24-25 describes a high mountain like a throne beside which stands the tree of life.
Greek and Asian cities often had acropolis temples on heights; Pergamum's temples crowned its hill.

The vantage point parallels 17:3, where John was carried 'in the Spirit' into a wilderness to see the harlot. The mountain also identifies the city with the cosmic mountain of God — Eden, Sinai and Zion fulfilled.
Shining with the glory of God; its radiance like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal
The glory of God returns to the temple in Ezekiel 43:2-5 and rises on Zion in Isaiah 60:1-2, 19. The Shekinah glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35).
The One on the throne looked like jasper (4:3); now the whole city shares his appearance. The city reflects God himself — the church as the bearer of his glory.
A great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates

Ezekiel 48:30-35: the city's twelve gates, three on each side, bear the names of the tribes. Isaiah 26:1 (salvation as walls) and Isaiah 62:6 (watchmen on Jerusalem's walls). The Qumran New Jerusalem texts and Temple Scroll (11QT 39-41) also assign tribal names to twelve gates.
Ancient city walls with monumental gates expressed security and civic identity; city gates were closed and guarded at night.

The city fulfils Israel's hope; whether the redeemed community inherits Israel's identity or national Israel keeps a distinct place within it is debated (see the readings). The angels act as gate-guardians or watchmen. John orders the gates east, north, south, west (Ezekiel lists north, east, south, west); proposed significances (e.g., a zodiacal or compass pattern) are speculative.
Dispensationalists see the tribal names as indicating the continuing distinct identity of national Israel alongside the church within the eternal city.
Amillennialists and progressive covenantalists see the tribes and apostles together (21:12-14) as the one people of God of both testaments, Israel's promises fulfilled in Christ's community.
Twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb

Isaiah 28:16 (a tested cornerstone in Zion); Isaiah 54:11 (foundations laid with sapphires). The Qumran Community Rule (1QS 8:1-10) describes a council of twelve men as a living foundation and precious cornerstone.
Building inscriptions in Greco-Roman cities honoured founders and benefactors on foundations and walls.

Twelve tribes on the gates plus twelve apostles on the foundations totals twenty-four, recalling the twenty-four elders (4:4). The church is built on the apostolic foundation (Ephesians 2:20) while entered through the gates of Israel's promises.
A golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls

Ezekiel's guide measures the temple with a measuring reed (Ezekiel 40:3-5 onward); Zechariah 2:1-5 shows a man with a measuring line for Jerusalem, which will be a city without walls with God as a wall of fire. The Qumran New Jerusalem texts are largely a record of an angel's measurements.
Surveyors laid out Roman colonies and Hellenistic cities with measuring rods; Hippodamian planning prized regular, measured grids.
Measuring signifies protection, ownership and the secure establishment of what God has built (compare 11:1-2, where John measured the temple). Gold marks the instrument fit for a holy place.
The city lies foursquare… 12,000 stadia in length and width and height

The Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple was a perfect cube, twenty cubits each way, overlaid with gold (1 Kings 6:20). Ezekiel's temple and city are square (Ezekiel 45:2; 48:16-20). The Qumran New Jerusalem texts describe a vast rectangular city.

Herodotus (1.178) described Babylon as a square city; ancient cities were often measured by circumference. A stadion was about 185-192 metres, so 12,000 stadia is roughly 2,200 km (about 1,400-1,500 miles) — roughly the distance across much of the Roman Mediterranean world.

The whole city is a Holy of Holies, the place of God's immediate presence, now as large as the known world. 12,000 is 12 (the people of God) x 1,000 (fullness). Most commentators read the dimensions symbolically; the sheer height has led some literalists to propose a pyramid shape.
Literal futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) take the measurements as the actual dimensions of the future city, allowing that its height may suit glorified life in the new creation.
Idealists and most amillennial commentators (Beale) read the cube as a symbol: the whole people of God become the Holy of Holies, God's presence filling the new creation.
Partial preterists such as Chilton read it as the church as God's temple-city now growing to fill the world, its perfect form showing its completeness and holiness.
Its wall 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using
144 = 12 x 12, echoing the 144,000 of Israel's tribes (7:4; 14:1). A cubit was about 45-52 cm (forearm length).
Roman and Hellenistic city walls were typically a few metres thick and ten to twenty metres high; 144 cubits (about 65-75 metres) would be enormous for a wall, yet tiny against a 2,200-km-high city.

Whether thickness or height is meant is unclear. The disproportion suggests symbolism: the wall signals perfect security and the completeness of the people of God. 'Human measure… angel's' perhaps means the measure is understandable to humans though used by an angel.
The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass

Solomon overlaid the temple and Holy of Holies with pure gold (1 Kings 6:20-22, 30). Tobit 13:16-17 foresees Jerusalem's towers and battlements of pure gold and streets paved with ruby and stones of Ophir.

Ancient glass was usually cloudy; perfectly transparent glass was a marvel. Gold was the standard of wealth and was used to gild temples and imperial statues; Nero's 'Golden House' (Domus Aurea) after AD 64 epitomised imperial luxury.

Gold transparent as glass is an impossible material, signalling a reality beyond earthly experience — purity and glory without any concealment. The whole city, including its main street (21:21), is a holy sanctuary.
The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone

Three backgrounds combine. (1) The high priest's breastpiece of judgment carried twelve stones engraved with the tribes' names (Exodus 28:17-21; 39:10-14); eight of John's twelve names (sardion, topazion, smaragdos, sappheiros, iaspis, amethystos, chrysolithos, bēryllion) appear in the Septuagint list, though in a different order. (2) Isaiah 54:11-12 promises Zion foundations of sapphires, battlements of rubies and gates of jewels. (3) Ezekiel 28:13 lists precious stones covering the figure in Eden. Josephus (Antiquities 3.186; Jewish War 5.234) and Philo (Special Laws 1.87; Life of Moses 2.124) link the breastpiece stones to the twelve months or the signs of the zodiac. Tobit 13:16-17 also has a jewelled Jerusalem.

Precious stones were luxury imports from India, Arabia, Egypt and beyond, carved into signets and cameos and worn by the elite; Pliny the Elder's Natural History Book 37 catalogues them. R. H. Charles argued that John's list runs in reverse order of the zodiac signs, as a rejection of astrology; this is widely disputed because ancient lists of zodiacal stones varied.

The city is built like the high priest's breastpiece: the whole people of God is the priestly bearer of his presence, every member precious. The Edenic echo makes the city a restored garden-sanctuary. The exact identity of several ancient stone names is uncertain.
Literal futurists expect real gemstones in the future city's foundations, displaying God's glory.
Symbolic readers (Beale, Hendriksen) focus on the priestly and Edenic meanings: the redeemed as a royal priesthood, beautiful and enduring.
The first foundation was jasper
Jasper (Hebrew yashpheh) is the twelfth stone of the breastpiece in the Hebrew text (Exodus 28:20); the Septuagint places iaspis sixth (Exodus 28:18). It also appears in Ezekiel 28:13.

Ancient 'jasper' covered various opaque or translucent stones, often green; Pliny (Natural History 37) describes many colours. John's 'clear as crystal' jasper (21:11) does not match modern opaque jasper, and some suggest rock crystal or even diamond.
Jasper is the stone that describes God's own appearance (4:3), the city's radiance (21:11) and its wall (21:18). Placed first, it marks the whole city with God's glory.
The second, sapphire

Under God's feet at Sinai was a pavement like sapphire (Exodus 24:10); Ezekiel's throne looked like sapphire (Ezekiel 1:26; 10:1); Isaiah 54:11 promises foundations of sapphires — the nearest background for this foundation. The fifth stone of the breastpiece in the Septuagint.
Ancient sappheiros was most likely lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone flecked with gold-like pyrite, imported from Afghanistan (Pliny, Natural History 37).
The colour of the heavens and of the throne-room floor: the city is founded on the vision of God's throne and fulfils Isaiah's sapphire foundations.
The third, chalcedony
Chalcedony does not appear in the breastpiece lists or elsewhere in the Bible; its inclusion is one of John's departures from Exodus 28.

Named after Chalcedon on the Bosphorus, opposite Byzantium. Its ancient identity is uncertain: possibly a greenish copper-bearing stone Pliny calls the 'Chalcedonian emerald' (Natural History 37), or the milky-blue quartz now called chalcedony.
Mostly contributes to the whole picture of varied, brilliant colour; no specific symbolism is clearly established.
The fourth, emerald

Smaragdos is the third stone of the breastpiece in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:17) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13 and Tobit 13:16 (Jerusalem built with sapphire and emerald). The rainbow round God's throne looked like emerald (Revelation 4:3).

Pliny ranks the emerald third among gems and says its green rests the eyes; he reports that Nero watched gladiator fights reflected in an emerald (Natural History 37). Egyptian emerald mines were worked in Roman times.
Linked with the rainbow of the throne — the sign of God's covenant faithfulness after judgment (Genesis 9) — now built into the city's foundations.
The fifth, sardonyx

Not listed by that name in the Septuagint breastpiece list, though onyx stones engraved with the tribes' names sat on the high priest's shoulders (Exodus 28:9-12) and onyx is one of the breastpiece stones (Exodus 28:20).
